prompt: Explain the UNFCCC and the annual COP meetings.
hook: Almost every country is in the room.

card.oneLiner: The UNFCCC is the 1992 treaty under which countries meet each year at the Conference of the Parties (COP) to negotiate climate action.
keyPoints: Nearly every country is a party to the convention.
The COP is the decision-making meeting of those parties.
Decisions are usually taken by consensus.
India is an active party and hosts and shapes negotiations.

framework.name: UN Framework Convention on Climate Change
framework.gloss: The founding treaty and its principle of common but differentiated responsibilities.

framework.name: Conference of the Parties
framework.gloss: The supreme body that reviews and advances the convention.

whatYouCanDo: Follow India's submissions and statements to the UNFCCC.
Read the COP decision summaries rather than headlines alone.
Understand that pledges are national and voluntary in design.
card.caveats: Educational information, not professional advice. Negotiation outcomes evolve each year.

prompt: Explain the Paris Agreement and nationally determined contributions.
hook: Each country writes its own homework, then shows it.

card.oneLiner: The 2015 Paris Agreement has each country submit a nationally determined contribution (NDC) and update it every five years, aiming to hold warming well below 2°C.
keyPoints: Countries set their own targets rather than being assigned them.
NDCs are meant to be strengthened over time, not weakened.
A transparency system tracks progress.
The goal is well below 2°C and 1.5°C in reach.

framework.name: Paris Agreement
framework.gloss: Nationally determined contributions and the ambition cycle.

whatYouCanDo: Look up what your country actually pledged.
Check whether the pledges add up to the temperature goal.
card.caveats: Educational information, not professional advice. Pledges and their accounting change over time.

prompt: Explain loss and damage and the fund for climate-vulnerable countries.
hook: Some damage cannot be adapted away.

card.oneLiner: Loss and damage refers to climate impacts that go beyond what adaptation can prevent, and a dedicated fund now exists to help vulnerable countries.
keyPoints: The idea covers both economic and non-economic losses.
A mechanism was set up under the UNFCCC to address it.
A fund was agreed to channel support to vulnerable countries.
Who pays, and how much, remains contested.

framework.name: UNFCCC
framework.gloss: The workstream addressing impacts beyond adaptation.

framework.name: COP27 decision
framework.gloss: Agreement to establish a fund for vulnerable countries.

whatYouCanDo: Distinguish adaptation, mitigation and loss and damage.
Follow how the fund is capitalised and governed.
Note India's interest as a highly vulnerable country.
card.caveats: Educational information, not professional advice. The fund's scale and rules are still developing.

prompt: Explain climate finance and the 100 billion dollar promise.

card.oneLiner: Developed countries pledged to mobilise 100 billion dollars a year to help developing countries cut emissions and adapt, and climate finance remains central to negotiations.
keyPoints: Finance is split between mitigation and adaptation.
The original pledge was for 100 billion dollars a year.
A new, larger goal is being negotiated.
India argues for finance that is additional and not loan-heavy.

framework.name: UNFCCC
framework.gloss: Obligations on developed countries to provide support.

framework.name: COP finance decisions
framework.gloss: Negotiations on a post-2025 finance target.

whatYouCanDo: Track how much finance is grants versus loans.
Note the gap between adaptation needs and money delivered.
Follow India's finance demands at the COP.
card.caveats: Educational information, not professional advice. Definitions of climate finance are debated.

prompt: Explain what the IPCC is and how its reports are produced.
hook: The IPCC does not do new science; it reads all of it.

card.oneLiner: The IPCC is a UN body that assesses published climate science through expert authors and government review, producing reports like the Sixth Assessment Report.
keyPoints: It assesses existing research rather than running new studies.
Three working groups cover science, impacts, and mitigation.
Summaries are approved line by line by member governments.
Its reports inform negotiations without prescribing policy.

framework.name: IPCC
framework.gloss: Expert authors plus government review of summaries.

framework.name: IPCC AR6
framework.gloss: The latest full assessment at the time of writing.

whatYouCanDo: Read the Summary for Policymakers first.
Quote the report rather than second-hand summaries.
Note that IPCC reports are not policy prescriptions.
card.caveats: Educational information, not professional advice. New assessment cycles supersede older findings.
